name: Affirmations / self-talk
lead: Affirmations and self-talk are mental practices in which a person repeats, writes or silently says encouraging statements, or reflects on personal values, to change how they see and speak to themselves. In looks-related use, people apply them to quiet harsh judgments of their face and body, aiming for steadier confidence that shows up as more upright posture, easier eye contact and a calmer social presence, and for the consistency that keeps training, skincare and grooming routines going.[1][2][3]

Two separate traditions sit under the same name. Positive affirmations come from the New Thought and self-help movement, running from Wallace Wattles' 1910 book The Science of Getting Rich through Louise Hay's 1984 You Can Heal Your Life to Rhonda Byrne's 2006 The Secret.[1] Self-affirmation theory is an academic framework proposed by the social psychologist Claude Steele in 1988, in which people reflect on important values to protect their sense of self-worth under threat.[2][4] A third body of work, from sport psychology, studies the instructional and motivational phrases athletes say to themselves.[5][8]

Research on each strand exists, but none has measured facial or physical appearance as an outcome. Studies describe lower stress responses and less defensiveness after value-based self-affirmation,[2][4] a moderate performance benefit from sport self-talk,[5] and a 2009 finding by Wood and colleagues that repeating present-tense positive statements helped people with high self-esteem and left people with low self-esteem feeling worse.[14] Lifters on forums such as T Nation describe self-talk mainly as a way to get through demanding sessions.[18][19]

angle.text: People use affirmations and self-talk to quiet negative body-image thoughts and to feel more at ease with their appearance. Some also use self-talk to push through training sessions, which feeds into physique goals.

paras: In the New Thought and New Age sense, an affirmation is a carefully worded statement repeated aloud or silently and often written down. Teachers commonly describe effective ones as present tense, positive, personal and specific.[1] Practitioners also use affirming images, words and videos, classes and lectures, mantra chanting, and hypnosis; the practice appears in neuro-linguistic programming and in the 'neuro-associative conditioning' popularised by Anthony Robbins.[1]

Wikipedia traces the modern movement through Wallace Wattles' 1910 The Science of Getting Rich, which inspired Rhonda Byrne, and through Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich, which expresses similar ideas.[1] Louise Hay, a Religious Science practitioner, published You Can Heal Your Life in 1984; her affirmations aim to replace beliefs she thought supported illness with beliefs she thought supported healing.[1] Byrne's 2006 book and film The Secret brought the idea of the law of attraction to a mass audience.[1] The belief behind these traditions is summed up in the article as a conviction that a positive mental attitude supported by affirmations will achieve success in anything.[1]

Some teachers add conditions. Esther Hicks, author of the Law of Attraction books, recommends using affirmations when one is already happy and at peace, and Rhonda Britten suggests pairing them with 'acknowledgements', records of steps already taken, so that attention goes to progress rather than self-criticism. Her example is noting the purchase of gym clothes in support of a weight-loss goal.[1]

Self-affirmation theory was popularised by Claude Steele in the late 1980s, building on his 1988 chapter 'The Psychology of Self-Affirmation'. Its central idea is that people are motivated to protect their self-integrity, a sense of being good, adequate and moral, and that a threat in one area can be offset by affirming a strength in another.[2] Sherman and Cohen's 2006 review extended the framework.[2]

In experiments, participants typically rank values such as aesthetic, social, political, religious, economic and theoretical, and then write for about five minutes on a top-ranked value, or complete a values scale.[2] Cohen and Sherman's 2014 Annual Review of Psychology article describes the technique as writing about core personal values, which produces a more expansive view of the self and weakens the implications of a threat; the authors report benefits for education, health and relationships that sometimes persist for months or years.[4]

Reported findings include lower cortisol responses to a laboratory stressor (Creswell and colleagues, 2005), equal problem-solving performance for high-stress and low-stress students after affirmation (Creswell, 2013), and greater acceptance of a health-risk article among heavy coffee drinkers, for whom the threat was personal (Sherman, Nelson and Steele, 2000).[2] Cohen and colleagues' school studies (2006, 2009) reported higher grades among affirmed minority seventh-graders over two years, and Logel and Cohen (2012) reported that weight-concerned women who completed a values essay lost more weight and had lower BMI and smaller waist circumference.[2]

Wikipedia notes limits and open questions: the mechanism has not been identified; results on mood and self-esteem are mixed; effects vary across cultures, with Heine and Lehman (1997) finding reduced dissonance for individualist but not collectivist participants; many studies use undergraduates; benefits appear mainly when the threatened domain matters to the person; and the stress findings are described as preliminary.[2] A pilot trial in end-stage renal disease reported better phosphate control after affirmation.[2]

sections.h: Positive self-statements and the 'I am' format
paras: The best-known test of repeated present-tense statements is Wood, Perunovic and Lee's 2009 paper in Psychological Science. A survey found that people often use positive self-statements and believe they work. In two experiments, participants with low self-esteem who repeated a statement such as 'I am a lovable person' felt worse than those who did not, as did those who dwelt on how the statement was true, while participants with high self-esteem felt somewhat better. The authors concluded the statements may help some people but may backfire for those who most need them.[14] Wikipedia adds that people with low self-esteem fared better with statements that allowed for doubt or were future-tense, such as 'I will'.[1]

Later work has looked at brain responses and combinations with other methods. Wikipedia reports a 2016 fMRI study by Cascio and colleagues in which self-affirmation engaged reward-related regions (the ventral striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex) and future-oriented affirmations were linked to objectively measured behaviour change, and a 2024 paper associating affirmative practices combined with mindfulness with better emotional self-regulation.[1] A 2024 fMRI study of 21 adults found that hearing self-affirmation statements in one's own voice versus another voice engaged different brain regions, with greater precuneus involvement for the own-voice version.[16] A 2025 psychology paper examined belief in manifestation, the idea behind The Secret.[12]

Wikipedia distinguishes self-talk, a single voice addressing itself, from inner dialogue, in which several voices take turns. It describes instructional self-talk, which directs attention to the components of a task and can help while a physical skill is being learned but may hurt people already skilled at it, and coping self-talk, which emphasises strengths and skills without implying perfection and can help people calm down and set realistic goals.[13] Second-person ('you') phrasing is used more when people regulate themselves or face difficult actions, and in one study cited there second-person suggestions were more effective than other forms for promoting intentions to act.[13]

In cognitive behavioural therapy, negative core beliefs are thought to drive negative self-talk, and a key method is to notice these beliefs and question whether they are true. Mindfulness is a related approach that encourages evaluating experiences without judgment.[13]

Distanced self-talk is a research variant. A set of seven studies (585 participants) published in 2014 found that using one's own name or non-first-person pronouns during introspection improved thoughts, feelings and behaviour under social stress, including in socially anxious people.[9] A 2022 Scientific Reports paper reported that distanced self-talk increased rational self-interest in decision tasks.[22]

Sport psychology has measured self-talk directly. A meta-analysis of 32 studies (62 effect sizes) found a positive, moderate effect of self-talk on sport task performance.[5] A systematic review of 47 studies reported beneficial effects of positive, instructional and motivational self-talk, while also noting that negative self-talk did not impede performance in the studies analysed and that evidence for different effects of instructional versus motivational self-talk was inconsistent.[8] A 2005 study quantified the self-talk of athletes during competition.[21]

In a randomised between-group trial of endurance cycling, motivational self-talk reduced perceived effort and extended time to exhaustion.[6] The Wikipedia article on self-talk observes that sport psychology widely assumes positive self-talk helps and negative self-talk hinders, with some empirical support but not thorough research.[13]

Lifters describe the same practice in training logs. One T Nation poster wrote of a hard workout with 'lots of self-talk', said out loud, to get through all the work.[18] Another mentioned self-talk while pushing through sprints and a martial arts class that was a hard sell to himself.[19] A T Nation thread quotes a piece attributed to Brandon Webb on the importance of self-talk, framing it as a core training skill rather than 'airy-fairy' personal-growth talk.[20] The training chain is straightforward: sessions completed, then more total work, then physique change over months.

sections.h: How people use it for looks
paras: People who link affirmations to appearance describe a behavioural and presentational route rather than a change in facial or bodily structure. They report less self-criticism before social situations, more upright posture and steadier eye contact, and better follow-through on training, skincare and grooming routines. These reports are descriptions of what practitioners say, not measured outcomes.

The closest research concerns appearance-linked behaviour. Randomised trials have tested self-affirmation approaches for sun protection and for reducing defensiveness toward health-risk messages,[7][11] and Logel and Cohen's weight study is described on Wikipedia.[2] Distanced self-talk, tested under social stress in the 2014 studies, is the research variant most relevant to confidence in social situations.[9]

Wikipedia's article on body image links poor body image with lower self-esteem and with attempts to change the body through dieting or cosmetic surgery, and describes interventions such as school body-confidence lessons and body-positive media.[3] Studies of affirmation in this area have given mixed results. In a 2026 experiment with 250 college-aged women, viewing idealised influencer posts lowered body satisfaction and positive affect, and neither general nor body-positive self-affirmation writing tasks protected against the effect; the body-positive task may have worsened it.[15]

A 2025 randomised trial of 158 young Japanese women found that a combined intervention reducing the negative facet of self-compassion and increasing the positive facet reduced body dissatisfaction and improved self-esteem compared with control, a result related to, but distinct from, affirmation.[17] Self-compassion, mindfulness and cognitive-behavioural methods are the neighbouring practices that body-image researchers more often test.

No studies found testing affirmations for physical appearance outcomes. Related randomised trials and reviews cover self-affirmation for stress, performance and health behaviour,[4][7][11] self-talk for sport performance,[5][6][8] and the 2009 and 2026 experiments on positive statements and body satisfaction described above.[14][15]

lore.intro: In training and self-improvement forums, affirmations and self-talk come up as a mindset tool, usually in terms of motivation, discipline and confidence rather than facial structure.[10][18][19]

claims.claim: Positive self-talk helps you push harder and stay confident
claims.believers: A T Nation lifter wrote that positive self-talk is very helpful and that it is worth overcompensating in that direction.[10] Others describe talking themselves through hard sessions out loud.[18][19]
claims.experts: A meta-analysis of 32 studies reported a moderate benefit of self-talk for sport performance, and a randomised cycling trial found motivational self-talk extended time to exhaustion.[5][6]

claims.believers: New Thought teachers present present-tense positive statements as the standard method.[1]
claims.experts: Wood and colleagues (2009) reported that such statements helped people with high self-esteem but worsened mood for those with low self-esteem.[14]

claims.claim: Future-tense or doubt-allowing statements work better for people who feel low
claims.believers: Teachers who adapt the method suggest wording that fits how the person actually feels, or pairing statements with acknowledgements of steps already taken.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia summarises the 2009 finding that people with low self-esteem fared better with statements allowing for doubt or using the future tense.[1]

claims.claim: Writing about your values makes you more resilient under pressure
claims.believers: Proponents of values affirmation describe it as a short exercise that lowers defensiveness and stress.[4]
claims.experts: Cohen and Sherman's review reports benefits in education, health and relationships, while Wikipedia calls the stress findings preliminary and notes the mechanism is unidentified.[4][2]

claims.claim: Talking to yourself by name or as 'you' calms you before social situations
claims.believers: Practitioners use second-person self-talk to manage nerves before difficult actions.[13]
claims.experts: Seven studies (N = 585) found non-first-person self-reference improved responses under social stress, including in socially anxious people.[9]

claims.claim: Affirmations protect body image against idealised social media
claims.believers: Body-positive affirmation is promoted as a way to feel better about one's looks.[3]
claims.experts: A 2026 experiment with 250 women found general and body-positive self-affirmation tasks did not protect body satisfaction after idealised influencer posts, and the body-positive task may have worsened it.[15]

claims.claim: Thoughts become reality through the law of attraction
claims.believers: The Secret and related New Thought works teach that positive mental attitude supported by affirmations achieves success in anything.[1]
claims.experts: A 2025 psychology paper examined belief in manifestation as a psychological phenomenon; no study has tested affirmations for changing physical appearance.[12]

card.summary: Repeating positive self-statements to shift self-image; value-based self-affirmation has some research, but nothing tests it for looks.
card.note: Present-tense statements may backfire for people with low self-esteem (Wood 2009).

quick.overview:
Affirmations are positive statements people repeat to change how they see themselves, sometimes used for face or body image.

Research on value-based self-affirmation shows stress-buffering effects that are described as preliminary, while a 2009 study found repeated positive statements can backfire for people with low self-esteem.
quick.mechanism: Self-affirmation theory proposes that reflecting on valued domains protects overall self-worth, which reduces defensiveness under threat.
quick.risks: No physical risks are documented. Studies suggest present-tense positive statements may worsen mood for people with low self-esteem.
